newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Perry expected in Kuwait to tighten noose on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Perry expected in Kuwait to tighten noose on Iraq.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry was due in Kuwait on Sunday on a mission to tighten Washington's military noose around Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
Western sources said they believed he stopped first in Saudi Arabia, Washington's main Arab ally and the dominate Gulf Arab power, ahead of his Kuwait visit.
Riyadh, eager thus far not to appear as being directly involved in the current U.S. military buildup in the Gulf, has kept silent on Perry's visit.

Kuwait, grateful to Washington for leading its 1991 Gulf War liberation from a seven-month Iraqi occupation, is so far the only Arab country to support the United States in its latest standoff with Saddam.
It has allowed added U.S. troops and military hardware to deploy in the tiny Gulf oil state.
Kuwait's government said in a statement to parliament: "This (Iraqi) regime does not understand anything but force and this regime will always create tension in the region."
Perry is on a regional tour to discuss possible future measures against Iraq, Kuwaiti Information Minister Sheikh Saud al-Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah said.

He did not spell out the measures. But a Western military analyst in Kuwait said Washington was keen to stress to its regional allies, some reluctant to get directly involved in the military buildup, the need to deal firmly with Saddam.
"The Americans want a free hand (in dealing with Iraq), there is no doubt about that," said the analyst. Washington "wants to make sure that no one messes with Uncle Sam in the Gulf."
While most of its regional allies are unwilling to take part, Washington is sending a second carrier battle group of warships to the region and had decided to dispatch another 5,000 troops to Kuwait.
CNN television reported on Sunday that the United States had put on hold its decision to send the extra soldiers but the report could not be independently confirmed.
Eight Stealth bombers landed in Kuwait on Friday for a possible military strike against Iraq.

The deployment was widely welcomed in Kuwait where many citizens informally celebrate former U.S. President George Bush's birthday and name their sons after the man who led the Gulf War coalition. Even a new luxury residential building overlooking the Gulf has been named after him.
President Bill Clinton said on Saturday he had placed a "strategic strait-jacket" on Saddam by sending enough military force to the Gulf to keep him in check.
Kuwait defended the large U.S. deployment on its territory, saying it was an act of sovereignty within the terms of defence pacts with Gulf War coalition states.

But the Arab League, which groups all Arabs states including Iraq and Washington's close allies in the Gulf, condemned U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq this month, saying they violated Iraqi sovereignty.

Analysts said Arab states were mainly concerned that a further weakened Baghdad or Saddam's downfall could result in Iraq's disintegration into three states -- a Kurdish north, a Shi'ite Moslem south and an Arab country in central Iraq.
"It is not out of love for Saddam (they take this stand), it is fear of making the problem even worse for everybody," including the West, one analyst said.

Kuwait's Sheikh Saud stressed he was not advocating Saddam's downfall but said: "The crisis will never be over until Saddam Hussein goes. This cat-and-mouse game has to stop...Some kind of measures will have to be taken to put an end to this."
The Central Intelligence Agency spent about $100 million since 1991 to implement a classified presidential order to oust Saddam, the Washington Post reported on Sunday.
Kuwaiti and Western officials said Iraq must do more to avert further U.S. strikes, including making all air defences in an expanded southern no-fly zone non-operational.
